Undo
ŭn-dū´
v. (to loose; to unfasten; to reverse what has been done)
From un- + do, Saxon undon, to unfasten. Scripture uses it twice, once of the burdens men are to loose from others, and once of what God will do to those who afflict His people.

Biblical Definition

Isaiah's great chapter on fasting defines the fast God chose in terms of what is loosed: “Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?” (Isaiah 58:6). The people had complained that God took no notice of their fasting, and He answers by describing a fast with no food in it at all. What follows is equally concrete: “Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?” (Isaiah 58:7). Zephaniah gives the word to God as His own action: “Behold, at that time I will undo all that afflict thee: and I will save her that halteth, and gather her that was driven out; and I will get them praise and fame in every land where they have been put to shame” (Zephaniah 3:19). And the promise attached to Isaiah's fast is light: “Then shall thy light break forth as the morning, and thine health shall spring forth speedily: and thy righteousness shall go before thee; the glory of the LORD shall be thy rereward” (Isaiah 58:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines undo as to reverse what has been done; to annul; to loose; to open what is shut or fastened.

expand to see more

UNDO, v.t. To reverse what has been done; to annul; to bring to naught.

UNDO, v.t. To loose; to open; to take to pieces; to unfasten; to unravel.

FAST, n. Abstinence from food, voluntarily, as a religious mortification or humiliation.

OPPRESS, v.t. To load or burden with unreasonable impositions; to treat with unjust severity or hardship.

YOKE, n. A piece of timber fitted to the necks of oxen; a mark of servitude; slavery; bondage.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 58:6 — "Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?"

Isaiah 58:7 — "Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?"

Zephaniah 3:19 — "Behold, at that time I will undo all that afflict thee: and I will save her that halteth, and gather her that was driven out; and I will get them praise and fame in every land where they have been put to shame."

Isaiah 58:8 — "Then shall thy light break forth as the morning, and thine health shall spring forth speedily: and thy righteousness shall go before thee; the glory of the LORD shall be thy rereward."

Modern Corruption

Isaiah 58 is claimed as a mandate for a social gospel detached from doctrine, or else neutralised into a chapter about personal devotional habits.

expand to see more

Isaiah 58 is fought over from both sides and rarely read as it stands. One party takes it as proof that God cares about justice and not about doctrine or worship, and builds a gospel of activism on it. But the chapter opens with God telling the prophet to cry aloud and shew His people their transgression, and it closes by commanding Sabbath-keeping and calling it a delight; it is a rebuke to false worship, not a replacement for worship. The people fasting in verse 3 were religiously observant and were smiting with the fist of wickedness on the same day.

The opposite party quietly reduces the chapter to interior piety — fast with the right attitude — and skips the list. The list will not be skipped. Loose the bands, undo the heavy burdens, let the oppressed go free, break every yoke, deal thy bread to the hungry, bring the poor that are cast out to thy house, cover the naked, hide not thyself from thine own flesh. These are the biblical categories, and they are personal and costly rather than abstract and political. The Reformed tradition has always held that faith without works is dead and that works are never the ground of acceptance. Isaiah 58 assumes both and treats them as a single obedience.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nathar (H5425), to loose or undo; motah (H4133), a yoke-bar; asah (H6213), to do or deal with; tsom (H6685), a fast.

expand to see more

Hebrew nathar (H5425) — to loose, undo; Isaiah 58:6, undo the heavy burdens.

Hebrew motah (H4133) — a yoke-bar, burden; that ye break every yoke.

Hebrew tsom (H6685) — a fast; the fast God did not choose and the one He did.

Hebrew asah (H6213) — to do, deal with; Zephaniah 3:19, I will undo all that afflict thee.

Hebrew anah (H6031) — to afflict, oppress; the oppressed who are to go free.

Usage

"“To undo the heavy burdens” — the fast God chose."

"“Hide not thyself from thine own flesh” — the list made personal."

"“I will undo all that afflict thee” — the same verb as God's own act."
